transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah… I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I’ve been feeling kind of disconnected from the things that normally make me feel like me. Like, I usually go on these photography walks—nothing fancy, just around the neighborhood or little places I notice light hitting buildings a certain way—and I haven’t really been doing that. Or even wanting to start doing it.

And I mentor some kids, which usually gives me a lot of purpose, you know? I’m usually the one checking in, planning things, following up. Lately it’s been like there’s this heaviness around initiating anything. Even at work, I’m someone who keeps a clean calendar, keeps things organized, stays on top of the details—that’s kind of my whole thing—and even that has started to feel flat, like I’m just dragging myself through it.

It’s not that I don’t know these things matter to me. I do. They just don’t feel like they’re reaching me the same way, if that makes sense. So I thought… okay, maybe I shouldn’t just keep brushing this off.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… longer than I wanted to admit, honestly. I’d say about a year and three months, give or take. It didn’t feel like one clear day where everything changed, but looking back, it started after a family member’s health and behavior changed, and I kind of stepped into this role of coordinating things more—appointments, communication, keeping track of what needed to happen.

At first I thought I was just tired or adjusting, because it felt practical, like, “Okay, this is what needs to be done.” But over time it was like that sense of being weighed down just settled in and stayed. So yeah, roughly fifteen months.
Do you feel this started because of the stress around your family member’s illness and the responsibilities that came with it?

Yeah, I think so… at least that’s when I can trace it back to. It wasn’t like I woke up one morning and thought, “Something is wrong with me.” It was more that my family member’s health and behavior changed, and then I started taking on more of the coordinating—keeping track of things, making sure communication happened, that kind of stuff.

And at first I told myself it was just the situation, like anyone would feel stretched. But it’s been about a year and three months now, and it didn’t really lift after I got used to the responsibilities. So yes, I do think it started around that stress and everything that came with it.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

I don’t know if I’d call it “excessive,” exactly. I mean, I do worry, but it feels like it’s mostly tied to practical things—what needs to get done, whether I’ve forgotten something, whether I’m keeping up with responsibilities the way I’m supposed to.

It’s not like I’m sitting there worrying about every possible thing all day, at least I don’t think so. Sometimes my mind kind of loops around tasks or obligations, but I’ve always been someone who keeps track of details, so it’s hard for me to tell where normal planning ends and worry starts. So… maybe some, but I’m not sure it’s a lot of different things in that broad way you mean.
For the past two years, have you felt down or low on most days?

For the past two years? I’m not sure I’d say two full years, no. I mean, I’ve had low stretches, definitely, and lately it’s felt more noticeable, but when you say “most days” over two years, that feels hard for me to answer cleanly.

I tend to think in terms of what was going on around me at the time, so I can remember periods where I was just kind of getting through the day and not feeling great, but I don’t know that I was down or low most days for that whole span. I’d have to really look back month by month to say that, and I don’t want to overstate it.
During this past year, have you felt sad or down most of the day on more days than not?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, this past year has definitely had a heavier feeling to it at times, and I’ve had days where I felt kind of low or worn down emotionally. But “most of the day” and “more days than not” — that’s where I get stuck, because I don’t know if I’ve been tracking it that clearly.

Some days I’d feel down in the morning and then get pulled into work or responsibilities and not notice it as much. Other days I might feel okay for a while and then it would hit me later. So I don’t want to say yes if that means it was clearly there most of the day, most days. I’d say… I’ve had sadness or low mood during the year, but whether it meets that exact pattern, I’m not sure.
Before this past year, was there ever another period in your life when you felt this same kind of loss of interest or low mood for at least two weeks?

Before this past year… I mean, I’ve had times where I was low before, but the thing that really made me come in now is more this feeling that the things that usually make me feel like myself started feeling flat. Like, I usually like going on photography walks — not in some grand artistic way, just walking around noticing light and buildings and little details — and I stopped initiating that. It started to feel heavy, like another obligation instead of something that gave me something back.

And mentoring the kids, too… that’s usually important to me. I’m usually the person who follows up, checks in, helps them think through stuff. But lately even that felt kind of muted, like I cared in principle but couldn’t really get myself to start. Even keeping a clean calendar — which sounds small, but for me that’s part of feeling organized and like myself — started feeling strangely burdensome instead of satisfying.

So, if you mean before this past year, another clear two-week stretch exactly like this… I’m not sure. I’ve had low periods, yes, but this particular flatness and not starting the things I normally care about is what’s been standing out more recently.
Have these feelings made it hard for you to function in your daily life?

Yeah… somewhat. I wouldn’t say everything has fallen apart, because it hasn’t. I’m still getting to work, and from the outside I probably look pretty functional. My work has stayed intact overall.

But I do notice these little slips that bother me because they’re not really like me. I work with calendars and details, so normally certain things are almost automatic — checking times, confirming appointments, keeping track of follow-ups. Lately I’ve missed a few calendar details, or I’ll catch myself needing to double-check something I normally would’ve just handled without thinking. It’s not catastrophic, but it makes me feel less steady, like I can’t fully trust my usual rhythm.

And outside of work, I’ve pulled back more. Photography walks used to be something I’d just do naturally, and I haven’t really been initiating those. With mentoring, too, I still care about it, but I don’t feel as present or reliable as I usually would, so I’ve kind of stepped back instead of pushing myself and then not following through. So yes, it has made daily life harder, just in a quieter way rather than a total collapse.
Before this past 15-month period, was there ever a time in your life when you felt this same kind of loss of interest or low mood nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m not sure I can say that clearly. I’ve definitely had periods before this where I felt low or less engaged, but when you say “nearly every day for at least two weeks,” I start second-guessing it, because I don’t think I was measuring it that way at the time.

There were times in the past where I’d get withdrawn or feel like I was just going through the motions, but I can’t confidently say it was the same kind of loss of interest, nearly every day, for a full two weeks or more. This more recent stretch is the one I can describe better because it’s been more noticeable to me — like the things I usually enjoy or keep up with started feeling harder to initiate.

So… I guess my honest answer is I don’t know. I wouldn’t want to say yes and make it sound more definite than it is.
During this 15-month period, was there ever a stretch of at least two weeks when you had little or no interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

Yes… during this 15-month period, yes. That’s probably the clearest part of what’s been going on.

It wasn’t like one dramatic day where I woke up and everything was gone, but there were definitely stretches — more than two weeks — where almost every day the things that usually make me feel like myself just felt flat. Photography walks are a good example because that’s usually something I don’t have to force. I’ll notice the light on a building or some little detail on a sidewalk and want to go out, but during that period I just… didn’t initiate it. It felt heavy, like another task on the list instead of something that gives me a little spark.

And mentoring the kids, too. That normally matters to me a lot, and I still knew it mattered, but I didn’t feel that pull to reach out or follow up the way I usually do. Even keeping a clean calendar — which sounds minor, I know — usually gives me this sense of order, like I’m on top of my life. But it started feeling burdensome instead of satisfying.

So yes, there were definitely periods of at least a couple weeks where interest and pleasure were low nearly every day. That’s really what made me feel like something was off enough to come in.
Is the family stress you mentioned still going on right now?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I don’t know if I’d call it “still going on” in the same way. Some of it is kind of just… in the background, if that makes sense. It’s not like there’s one active crisis every day that I can point to and say, “That’s the stress.” But I also wouldn’t say it’s completely resolved and no longer affecting me.

I guess I’d say there are still family-related things that feel unsettled, but I’m not sure how much they’re actively driving what I’m feeling right now versus just being part of the overall noise in my life. Sometimes I only realize it’s weighing on me after the fact, like I’ll be more tense or preoccupied and then think, “Oh, maybe that conversation or situation is still sitting with me.”

So… yes and no. It’s not as immediate as it may have been at certain points, but I don’t think it’s gone either.
Before this past 15-month period, was there ever a time when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Before this past 15 months… I still don’t feel like I can say yes to that confidently. I mean, I’ve had times in my life where I was less enthusiastic or kind of pulled back from things, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as depressed or losing interest nearly every day for two weeks. I wasn’t really tracking it that way, and I don’t want to make it sound more definite than it was.

What made me come in now is that this felt different enough for me to notice it. The things that usually make me feel like myself — going out for photography walks, mentoring the kids, even just keeping my calendar clean and organized — started feeling flat and heavy. Like they weren’t giving me that normal sense of satisfaction, and I just stopped initiating them. Not because I decided they didn’t matter, but because they felt like effort in a way they usually don’t.

So for before this period, I’d say I’m not sure. For this more recent period, yes, that loss of interest was clear.
Even on days when the family situation feels relatively calm, do you still feel this loss of interest?

Yes. I think that’s actually part of what made it feel like it wasn’t just about the family situation.

Even on days where nothing especially bad is happening, or things are relatively quiet, I still find myself not reaching for the things I normally would. Like, if the house is calm or I don’t have some stressful conversation hanging over me, you’d think I’d want to go take photos or get caught up with mentoring or straighten out my calendar and feel a little better from it. But a lot of the time it still feels flat. Heavy, almost.

It’s not that I decided those things don’t matter anymore. I still know they matter to me. I can explain why they matter. I just don’t initiate them the way I used to, and when I think about doing them, it feels more like pushing myself through a task than being drawn toward something I enjoy. So yes, even when the family stuff is quieter, that loss of interest is still there.
During this past 15-month period, have you felt sad or down nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m not sure I can answer that cleanly. I know there have been stretches where I felt low, or kind of emotionally weighed down, but “sad or down nearly every day for at least two weeks” is harder for me to pin down.

Part of the problem is that I don’t always experience it as obvious sadness, like crying or thinking, “I’m depressed today.” Sometimes it’s more like I’m moving through the day with less color in it, if that makes sense. But whether that was nearly every day for two full weeks… I honestly don’t know. I wasn’t marking the days, and I don’t want to just say yes because it sounds like it might fit.

I can say there were definitely periods during these 15 months where I felt off and lower than normal, but I’m not confident about the frequency or the exact duration in the way you’re asking.
During this 15-month period, have you had a significant change in your appetite?

I don’t think I’ve noticed a significant change, no. I mean, not in a way where I could say, “My appetite clearly went up,” or “I stopped eating,” or anything like that.

There are days where I eat more casually or I don’t pay much attention, but that’s not unusual for me depending on how busy the day is. And there are days where food just feels kind of like something I have to fit in, but I wouldn’t say my appetite itself changed dramatically. I haven’t had a clear pattern where I’m much hungrier than usual or not hungry for long stretches.

So I’d probably say no, or at least not that I’ve noticed in any meaningful way.
During this 15-month period, have you had trouble sleeping?

Yes, I have had trouble sleeping, though it’s a little strange because it isn’t always the kind where I’m lying there miserable all night.

There have been nights where I only sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I wake up before dawn — like really early — and instead of feeling exhausted the way I would expect, I feel like I could just get up and start doing things. I’ll think about answering emails or updating appointment lists, checking details, organizing something work-related, that kind of thing. It’s not like I wake up and think, “Oh no, I can’t sleep,” exactly. Sometimes it feels more like my mind is already switched on and ready to go.

It’s noticeable because normally if I only slept that little, I’d assume I’d be dragging, but on those nights I don’t always feel tired right away. I just get this early-morning readiness, almost like the day has started before it should have. So yes, during this period there have definitely been nights like that.
During those times when you slept only two or three hours and woke up ready to go, did you also feel unusually good, energized, or more confident than usual?

Yes… I think so. Not every single time, but there are definitely stretches where I feel unusually upbeat, like things are just clicking into place in a way they normally don’t. I’ll wake up early after barely sleeping and feel like, okay, I know exactly what needs to be done, I can handle all of it, everything is organized in my head.

And I do feel more confident during those times, probably more than is typical for me. It’s not always some huge dramatic feeling, but it’s like I’m more sure of myself, like I don’t second-guess every little thing. I’ll feel very on top of things.

But the other side of it is that I can get sharp really quickly. Like if I’m in that mode and someone changes a meeting time or moves something around, even something small, I can react with more edge than I mean to. I’ll hear myself being short with someone and think afterward, “Why did I say it like that?” It surprises me because in the moment it feels like they’ve disrupted the whole flow, even if objectively it’s just a minor change. So yes, there’s that upbeat, energized, confident part, but it can flip into irritability pretty fast over little things.
When you have those periods of needing only two or three hours of sleep and feeling unusually energized, do they last at least four days in a row?

Yes, they do. I mean, not like every single week on a perfect schedule, but those stretches where I’m sleeping only a couple hours and still feel really driven or overly confident — they can go on for several days in a row, yes. Four days would definitely fit some of them.

And it’s been something that keeps coming back. I’d say I’ve been having those elevated, kind of pushed-forward periods for maybe around eleven months now. It’s not just one isolated weekend where I stayed up too late or had too much coffee or something. It’s more like these recurring runs where I don’t seem to need much sleep, and I feel unusually ready to take things on, like I can handle more than usual. Then after a while it settles down, but it comes back again.
During those energized periods, do you find yourself starting a lot more projects or activities than usual?

Yes, definitely. During those stretches I sort of… I don’t just do one thing, I start opening up everything at once.

Like at work, I’ll decide the templates we use need to be rebuilt or cleaned up, so I’ll start making new versions of those. Then while I’m doing that, I’ll think, well, the files are a mess too, so I’ll start reorganizing folders and renaming things and making lists of what needs updating. And then I’ll remember care plans or appointment-related stuff that could be clearer, so I’ll start working on that too.

It isn’t just work either. I’ll start emailing relatives, trying to coordinate things or explain plans or check in on people, and it feels very urgent in the moment, like if I don’t handle it right then, I’m somehow dropping the ball. I can have several things going at the same time — templates, care plans, emails, files — and I’ll feel like sitting still would be irresponsible, almost. Like I need to keep moving from one task to the next because everything suddenly seems important and fixable.

patient.answer:
Before this past year… I mean, I’ve had times where I was low before, but the thing that really made me come in now is more this feeling that the things that usually make me feel like myself started feeling flat. Like, I usually like going on photography walks — not in some grand artistic way, just walking around noticing light and buildings and little details — and I stopped initiating that. It started to feel heavy, like another obligation instead of something that gave me something back.

And mentoring the kids, too… that’s usually important to me. I’m usually the person who follows up, checks in, helps them think through stuff. But lately even that felt kind of muted, like I cared in principle but couldn’t really get myself to start. Even keeping a clean calendar — which sounds small, but for me that’s part of feeling organized and like myself — started feeling strangely burdensome instead of satisfying.

So, if you mean before this past year, another clear two-week stretch exactly like this… I’m not sure. I’ve had low periods, yes, but this particular flatness and not starting the things I normally care about is what’s been standing out more recently.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms cause clinically significant impairment, which helps distinguish adjustment disorder from a depressive disorder when duration and trigger are unclear.
doctor.question: Have these feelings made it hard for you to function in your daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My work has stayed intact overall, but I’ve missed calendar details and had to double-check tasks that used to be automatic. I’ve also pulled back from photography outings and mentoring because I don’t feel as present or reliable.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the feelings have interfered with daily functioning, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… somewhat. I wouldn’t say everything has fallen apart, because it hasn’t. I’m still getting to work, and from the outside I probably look pretty functional. My work has stayed intact overall.

But I do notice these little slips that bother me because they’re not really like me. I work with calendars and details, so normally certain things are almost automatic — checking times, confirming appointments, keeping track of follow-ups. Lately I’ve missed a few calendar details, or I’ll catch myself needing to double-check something I normally would’ve just handled without thinking. It’s not catastrophic, but it makes me feel less steady, like I can’t fully trust my usual rhythm.

And outside of work, I’ve pulled back more. Photography walks used to be something I’d just do naturally, and I haven’t really been initiating those. With mentoring, too, I still care about it, but I don’t feel as present or reliable as I usually would, so I’ve kind of stepped back instead of pushing myself and then not following through. So yes, it has made daily life harder, just in a quieter way rather than a total collapse.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had a distinct major depressive episode during the current 15-month period, which would help separate major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder or generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: During this 15-month period, was there ever a stretch of at least two weeks when you had little or no interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms

patient.answer:
Yes… during this 15-month period, yes. That’s probably the clearest part of what’s been going on.

It wasn’t like one dramatic day where I woke up and everything was gone, but there were definitely stretches — more than two weeks — where almost every day the things that usually make me feel like myself just felt flat. Photography walks are a good example because that’s usually something I don’t have to force. I’ll notice the light on a building or some little detail on a sidewalk and want to go out, but during that period I just… didn’t initiate it. It felt heavy, like another task on the list instead of something that gives me a little spark.

And mentoring the kids, too. That normally matters to me a lot, and I still knew it mattered, but I didn’t feel that pull to reach out or follow up the way I usually do. Even keeping a clean calendar — which sounds minor, I know — usually gives me this sense of order, like I’m on top of my life. But it started feeling burdensome instead of satisfying.

So yes, there were definitely periods of at least a couple weeks where interest and pleasure were low nearly every day. That’s really what made me feel like something was off enough to come in.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the stressor is still ongoing, which best distinguishes adjustment disorder from a depressive disorder at this point.
doctor.question: Is the family stress you mentioned still going on right now?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether the family stressor is still ongoing right now, but the symptom profile does not include a specific item for current family stress or psychosocial stressors.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I don’t know if I’d call it “still going on” in the same way. Some of it is kind of just… in the background, if that makes sense. It’s not like there’s one active crisis every day that I can point to and say, “That’s the stress.” But I also wouldn’t say it’s completely resolved and no longer affecting me.

I guess I’d say there are still family-related things that feel unsettled, but I’m not sure how much they’re actively driving what I’m feeling right now versus just being part of the overall noise in my life. Sometimes I only realize it’s weighing on me after the fact, like I’ll be more tense or preoccupied and then think, “Oh, maybe that conversation or situation is still sitting with me.”

So… yes and no. It’s not as immediate as it may have been at certain points, but I don’t think it’s gone either.

Ongoing but not clearly time-limited family stress keeps F43.2 in the differential, while depressive disorders remain possible; recurrentity is still unclear, so both F32.9 and F33.9 stay.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is another core major depressive symptom, specifically sleep disturbance, to help distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder and support single-episode vs recurrent MDD assessment later.
doctor.question: During this 15-month period, have you had trouble sleeping?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: There have been nights when I sleep two or three hours, wake up before dawn, and feel ready to answer emails or update appointment lists instead of feeling tired.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly about sleep during the 15-month period, and the relevant profile item describes periods of sleeping only two or three hours while still feeling ready and energized.

patient.answer:
Yes, I have had trouble sleeping, though it’s a little strange because it isn’t always the kind where I’m lying there miserable all night.

There have been nights where I only sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I wake up before dawn — like really early — and instead of feeling exhausted the way I would expect, I feel like I could just get up and start doing things. I’ll think about answering emails or updating appointment lists, checking details, organizing something work-related, that kind of thing. It’s not like I wake up and think, “Oh no, I can’t sleep,” exactly. Sometimes it feels more like my mind is already switched on and ready to go.

It’s noticeable because normally if I only slept that little, I’d assume I’d be dragging, but on those nights I don’t always feel tired right away. I just get this early-morning readiness, almost like the day has started before it should have. So yes, during this period there have definitely been nights like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the decreased need for sleep is accompanied by elevated or expansive mood, which would suggest a bipolar-spectrum episode rather than a depressive or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During those times when you slept only two or three hours and woke up ready to go, did you also feel unusually good, energized, or more confident than usual?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I have stretches where I feel unusually upbeat and sure everything is clicking, then a tiny change like someone moving a meeting can make me sharp with people in a way that surprises me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the short-sleep periods were accompanied by unusually good, energized, or confident mood, which most directly matches elevated or irritable mood during manic-like stretches.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. Not every single time, but there are definitely stretches where I feel unusually upbeat, like things are just clicking into place in a way they normally don’t. I’ll wake up early after barely sleeping and feel like, okay, I know exactly what needs to be done, I can handle all of it, everything is organized in my head.

And I do feel more confident during those times, probably more than is typical for me. It’s not always some huge dramatic feeling, but it’s like I’m more sure of myself, like I don’t second-guess every little thing. I’ll feel very on top of things.

But the other side of it is that I can get sharp really quickly. Like if I’m in that mode and someone changes a meeting time or moves something around, even something small, I can react with more edge than I mean to. I’ll hear myself being short with someone and think afterward, “Why did I say it like that?” It surprises me because in the moment it feels like they’ve disrupted the whole flow, even if objectively it’s just a minor change. So yes, there’s that upbeat, energized, confident part, but it can flip into irritability pretty fast over little things.

inference.note: Added F31.8 because the patient now reports episodic decreased need for sleep (2–3 hours without fatigue), increased energy/confidence, and irritability—suggestive of hypomanic symptoms. F43.2 is less likely since symptoms persist even when the stressor is quiet and mood-episode features are emerging.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy, decreased-sleep periods lasted at least 4 days, which would support hypomania and distinguish bipolar II/other bipolar disorder from unipolar depression.
doctor.question: When you have those periods of needing only two or three hours of sleep and feeling unusually energized, do they last at least four days in a row?

target_item.name: Manic Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The elevated, driven stretches with less sleep and too much confidence have been recurring for about eleven months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the energized, low-sleep mood episodes last, which is most directly about the duration of the manic episode pattern.

patient.answer:
Yes, they do. I mean, not like every single week on a perfect schedule, but those stretches where I’m sleeping only a couple hours and still feel really driven or overly confident — they can go on for several days in a row, yes. Four days would definitely fit some of them.

And it’s been something that keeps coming back. I’d say I’ve been having those elevated, kind of pushed-forward periods for maybe around eleven months now. It’s not just one isolated weekend where I stayed up too late or had too much coffee or something. It’s more like these recurring runs where I don’t seem to need much sleep, and I feel unusually ready to take things on, like I can handle more than usual. Then after a while it settles down, but it comes back again.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods include increased goal-directed activity, which would support hypomania/bipolar II over unipolar depressive disorders.
doctor.question: During those energized periods, do you find yourself starting a lot more projects or activities than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: During those stretches I start rebuilding work templates, making care plans, emailing relatives, and reorganizing files all at once, like sitting still would mean I’m dropping the ball.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during energized periods, the patient starts many more projects or activities than usual, which directly matches increased goal-directed activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. During those stretches I sort of… I don’t just do one thing, I start opening up everything at once.

Like at work, I’ll decide the templates we use need to be rebuilt or cleaned up, so I’ll start making new versions of those. Then while I’m doing that, I’ll think, well, the files are a mess too, so I’ll start reorganizing folders and renaming things and making lists of what needs updating. And then I’ll remember care plans or appointment-related stuff that could be clearer, so I’ll start working on that too.

It isn’t just work either. I’ll start emailing relatives, trying to coordinate things or explain plans or check in on people, and it feels very urgent in the moment, like if I don’t handle it right then, I’m somehow dropping the ball. I can have several things going at the same time — templates, care plans, emails, files — and I’ll feel like sitting still would be irresponsible, almost. Like I need to keep moving from one task to the next because everything suddenly seems important and fixable.

inference.note: Recurrent periods of decreased need for sleep, elevated/irritable mood, increased confidence, and increased goal-directed activity lasting at least 4 days support hypomanic episodes, ruling in bipolar II spectrum and ruling out unipolar depressive disorders.
